claims.claim: JWT authentication works by replacing server‑side session storage with a self‑contained, signed token that the client presents on each request
The client sends a POST /login request that includes a username and password in the request body
if they are valid, it creates a JSON Web Token (JWT)
The header identifies the signing algorithm (e.g., HS256 for symmetric cryptography or RS256/ES256 for asymmetric cryptography)
The payload contains user‑specific claims such as an identifier, name, issue date, and expiry date
The signature is computed over the header and payload using a secret key (for HS256) or a private key (for RS256)
A secret key is generated once, encoded in Base64, and stored (e.g., in the service’s configuration)
The same key (or the matching public key) is later used to verify the token’s signature
The signed JWT is returned to the client, which stores it (e.g., in memory or local storage)
For each protected request, the client places the JWT in the HTTP Authorization header using the Bearer scheme
The receiving service extracts the token
verifies the signature with the known secret/public key
checks standard claims such as expiration
if verification succeeds, treats the request as authenticated without needing a server‑side session record
the token can be validated independently by any service that trusts the same signing key
the same JWT can be used for single sign‑on across multiple applications of the same provider
